title: From Curry House to Global Brand: Indian Restaurants Are Becoming a Worldwide Business
excerpt: A new international restaurant congress and a wave of diaspora-driven expansion are remaking Indian dining from corner takeaway into premium global category.
body:
For most of its history abroad, Indian food traveled on the back of the neighborhood curry house — cheerful, cheap, reliable, and rarely taken seriously by the fine-dining establishment. That image is dissolving fast. In 2026, Indian cuisine is being reframed as a premium global business category, complete with international awards platforms, cross-border franchising, and chef-led brands chasing investors from London to New York. For the diaspora that built those first restaurants, it is a remarkable turn of the wheel.

## Context & Background

The clearest signal came in late May, when the Indian Restaurant Congress & Awards made its international debut at the Royal Lancaster London during India Week 2026. Organized by Scale Media International in association with Franchise India and Restaurant India, the event was explicitly pitched as the launch of a "global platform connecting the Indian restaurant and hospitality ecosystem" across major culinary hubs worldwide.

The backdrop is a category that has quietly become an economic heavyweight. The UK alone is home to more than 12,000 Indian restaurants, contributing an estimated 4 to 5 billion pounds a year and supporting over 100,000 jobs. Organizers described Indian cuisine as having "evolved far beyond the traditional curry house model into a globally respected category spanning Michelin-starred dining, premium casual concepts, chef-led brands, experiential hospitality, and scalable international restaurant businesses."

## Current Developments

The momentum is visible on multiple fronts. The newly launched Indian Culinary Diaspora, a global network of chefs' associations, debuted in London in May 2026, formalizing the professional web of Indian chefs and caterers working across the UK and beyond. Industry organizers point to diaspora demand, rising tourism, premiumisation, and cross-border franchising as the forces pushing Indian restaurant brands from London, Dubai, and Singapore to Toronto, Sydney, and New York.

The United States is a central stage for this premiumisation. The 2026 James Beard Awards — the so-called Oscars of American food — featured an unprecedented number of Indian and Indian-inspired restaurants and restaurateurs as semifinalists and finalists, from the Cal-India Collective in the Bay Area to Chai Pani's Meherwan and Molly Irani and modern Indian spots in Las Vegas, Arizona, and Washington. Whatever the final results, the sheer presence of Indian fare across categories marks how far the cuisine has climbed in critical esteem.

## Diaspora Impact

For NRIs, this shift is deeply personal. Many grew up in families that ran or worked in those first-generation curry houses and takeaways — businesses that funded educations and built communities but were often dismissed as downmarket. Watching Indian cuisine reframed as a Michelin-worthy, investor-courted global category is a form of overdue respect for that earlier hustle.

It also changes the diaspora dining experience. NRIs increasingly have access to ambitious, regionally specific Indian restaurants that go far beyond the generic "curry" menu — places serving Hyderabadi biryani, Kerala curries, and Goan coastal dishes with the same seriousness afforded French or Japanese cuisine. The risk, as the category premiumizes, is that the affordable neighborhood spots that anchored immigrant communities get squeezed out in favor of high-concept venues.

## What's Next

With the Indian Restaurant Congress planning to expand into other global food capitals after London, and franchising platforms actively courting Indian hospitality brands, expect more cross-border expansion and consolidation. The next few years will likely see established Indian restaurant brands raising capital to scale internationally, much as Western fast-casual chains once did. The curry house is not disappearing — but it is no longer the whole story. Indian food has become a global business, and the diaspora is both its origin and its biggest market.
